data.sourceWord: MCQ: Crime involving violence due to race or religion
data.targetWord: Hate crime — a crime motivated by hostility or prejudice towards a person's race, religion, disability, sexual orientation, or gender identity. Hate crimes cause particular harm because they target people for their identity. Most religious traditions strongly condemn such acts as a violation of human dignity.

examples.en-GB: AQA Q5.1 (1 mark) — Answer: C Hate crime

data.sourceWord: FOR: Religious believers should never support the death penalty
data.targetWord: Most religious traditions teach that life is sacred and belongs ultimately to God, not humans. Taking a life — even as punishment — usurps God's authority over life and death. The possibility of executing an innocent person makes it irreversible and morally catastrophic. Christian, Buddhist, and many Muslim scholars oppose it on these grounds.

examples.en-GB: AQA Q5.5 (12 marks) — Evaluate: 'Religious believers should never support the death penalty'

data.sourceWord: AGAINST: Some religious traditions permit the death penalty
data.targetWord: Some religious believers support the death penalty for the most serious crimes, citing justice and protection of society. Qur'an 5:32 permits capital punishment for murder ('life for life'). The Old Testament prescribes the death penalty for numerous offences. Retribution for the most heinous crimes may be seen as just.

examples.en-GB: AQA Q5.5 (12 marks) — Arguments permitting the death penalty in religious thought

data.sourceWord: MCQ: Best description of the meaning of prejudice
data.targetWord: Prejudice means judging someone without knowing them — forming an opinion about a person or group based on preconceptions rather than facts. This is distinct from discrimination (acting unfairly) or stereotyping. Religious traditions strongly oppose prejudice as it denies the equal worth of all human beings.

examples.en-GB: AQA Q6.1 (1 mark) — Answer: B Judging someone without knowing them

data.sourceWord: FOR: Freedom of religion is the most important human right
data.targetWord: Freedom of religion is foundational to human dignity and identity because it concerns the deepest convictions about meaning, morality and ultimate reality. Many religious believers argue that without this freedom, individuals cannot fulfil their ultimate purpose — to worship God and live according to their conscience. It underpins all other freedoms.

examples.en-GB: AQA Q6.5 (12 marks) — Evaluate: 'The right to follow a religion is the most important human right'

data.sourceWord: AGAINST: Other rights may be more fundamental
data.targetWord: Some argue that rights to life, food, shelter and freedom from torture are more fundamental than religious freedom — one cannot practise religion if one is dead, starving or being tortured. Rights to equality and freedom from discrimination may also be seen as more universally applicable across religious and non-religious people.

examples.en-GB: AQA Q6.5 (12 marks) — Arguments against 'religious freedom is the most important right'
